Hassett says CPI data shows inflation needs ‘some work’
article:
(Oct 19): White House National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said prices have been falling for items such as beef and eggs, though consumer price data for September shows overall inflation continues to need policy attention.

“If you look at the previous three months, it looked like inflation was completely under control, and now it looks like it’s sort of back needing some work,” Hassett told CNBC on Monday.

Data last week showed consumer prices advanced in September at the fastest pace in five months and a gauge of underlying price pressures rose by more than expected. The consumer price index rose 0.6% from a month earlier while a key measure of underlying price pressures, which excludes food and energy, was up 0.3%.

“This is either a sort of break from the downtrend or a blip,” Hassett said in the interview.

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh last week did nothing to dispel market expectations that the central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month. In a moderated discussion at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, Warsh made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, apart from reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability.

Hassett said he respects the central bank’s independence and said Warsh will “do what he thinks is the right thing.”

“People are really euphoric about how well the economy is doing, and they’re spending more. And of course, that’s the kind of thing the Fed needs to pay attention to,” Hassett said.

title: Farage challenger faces £37,000 bill after losing court case
article:
(Oct 19): A by-election candidate who sought to wind up Reform UK lost his case and was ordered by an insolvency judge to pay £37,000 of the party’s legal expenses.

Daniel Pocock, who stood as an independent candidate against Reform leader Nigel Farage in the Clacton-on-Sea by-election in August, said Reform owed him £5,009.21 to cover costs incurred while campaigning. He argued that Farage’s offer to cover the costs of organising the contest also obliged the party to pay candidates’ expenses.

When he received no response from Reform, Pocock issued a winding-up petition. He said that questions around whether the party would have to hand back recent donations, due to changes in the rules applying to overseas donors, raised “serious questions about whether the debtor is currently solvent.”

At a hearing in London’s High Court on Monday, lawyers for Reform argued that Farage had clearly been offering to pay any costs incurred by the taxpayer — not by his party’s rivals.

Adam Richardson, representing Reform, argued that Pocock had made “improper use” of insolvency proceedings to “bear down” on Reform and increase the money the party had to spend on the case, possibly for politically motivated reasons, by sending large amounts of communications and refusing to give his address when asked.

See also: UK said to raise taxes on banks in budget this month

Chief Insolvency and Companies Court Judge Nicholas Briggs said Farage’s offer to pay for the by-election would clearly be understood by reasonable people to be referring to costs incurred by the taxpayer, not individual candidates. Pocock had employed a risky strategy to try and recoup money from Reform, he said, adding: “That high-risk strategy has backfired.”

Briggs added that in such a case, it was standard practice for an unsuccessful petitioner such as Pocock to pay Reform’s legal costs, which he put at £37,000 plus value added tax.

Neither Pocock nor any representative attended court on Monday. In an emailed statement to Bloomberg after the judgment was delivered, Pocock — a software developer born in Australia — appeared to imply that he would not pay Reform’s legal costs as ordered.

See also: Airtel Money shares slip in debut after biggest London IPO in five years

“After the sight of masked men at British ports and a sacked former home secretary using social media to vilify volunteer lifeboat crews, I don’t feel any Australian could give money to Reform UK without violating Australian laws that prohibit Australian citizens from resourcing insurrections abroad,” he said, referring to controversial anti-immigration protests organised by right-wing groups in the UK over the last several months.

Reform has not been directly involved with those protests, and Farage has condemned the violent behaviour exhibited in some, though a number of the party’s local councillors have been identified in Facebook groups associated with the organisers.

Reform declined to comment on the outcome of the case.

Farage triggered the Clacton by-election following a series of revelations in the press about the probity of Reform’s funding. He said he wanted to be judged by voters rather than Parliament’s standards commissioner, who has launched an investigation into an undeclared £5 million sum Farage received from a party donor before his return to politics in 2024. He was reelected, while Pocock received 16 votes.

title: Singapore issues haze notices to three more Indonesian firms
article:
Singapore’s government issued notices to three more Indonesian firms suspected to be linked to haze-creating fires, as it steps up action to combat its worst air pollution in more than a decade.

PT Buana Megatama Jaya, PT Mananjung Hayak and PT Baratama Putra Perkasa will all be notified under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said in a statement on Monday. There are indications that smoke from fires on concessions held by all three companies in Kalimantan spread to the city-state, the agency said.

Singapore and Malaysia have been blanketed by toxic smog from the Indonesian wildfires in recent weeks, with the dry conditions that have exacerbated the blazes linked to a powerful El Niño weather pattern. Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong last week vowed to investigate companies responsible for the blazes and warned that those found culpable could face legal action.

The action on Monday follows notices sent to seven companies on Friday. The notified firms will be required to deploy firefighters to curb blazes on their concessions, the agency said. Under the transboundary haze law, Singaporean authorities can fine companies as much as $100,000 per day of pollution.

Buana Megatama Jaya is listed as a supplier to APP Group, one of the pulp and paper industry’s largest companies. Two of the companies notified on Friday were also suppliers to APP.

APP Group said in a written response that the notices issued by Singapore were preventive measures and did not constitute a finding of wrongdoing. The pulp and paper giant said it would work with relevant suppliers to contain fires, prevent further outbreaks and enforce its zero-burning policy, adding that it had invested nearly US$300 million in fire management over the past decade.

See also: RegCo queries SGX-listed Indonesian agri firms on cause and impact of haze

Buana Megatama Jaya could not be reached for comment. Mananjung Hayak and Baratama Putra Perkasa didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

The 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index reading — which the act tracks — was as high as 114 on Monday after, according to NEA data. That’s lower than last week, when levels in parts of the city topped 200. In Pangkalanbun, a town in Kalimantan, a gauge of particulate matter peaked at more than 1,000 on Monday, figures from the Indonesian meteorology agency show. Levels above 250 are deemed dangerous.

Singapore also sought to enforce the transboundary haze law in 2015, but the environment ministry said at the time it was having difficulty getting information from its Indonesian counterpart on firms suspected of illegal burning. A decade on, four companies continue to be under investigation. - Bloomberg
